---
title: "Earlier-versus-later Helmert contrasts"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Recall that a [coding column](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd) assigns one numerical weight to each category, and the coefficient meaning follows from those weights. [Helmert coding](helmert-coding.qmd) compares each later level with the average of the earlier levels. **Reverse Helmert coding** turns that sequence around: each earlier level is compared with the average of the levels that follow it. The numerical weights determine the comparison.

For the MALD syllable bands, reverse Helmert coding asks how each earlier band differs from the mean of all later bands. Deriving those comparisons from the contrast matrix also shows why fitted values agree with forward Helmert coding.

This direction suits a different question from ordinary Helmert coding: does the shortest band differ from all longer words, then does the two-syllable band differ from the remaining longer bands, and finally do three-syllable words differ from the open top band? The order must come from that hypothesis rather than from the name of the coding scheme.

The basic idea is to reverse which side of the ordered list supplies the average. Ordinary Helmert coding asks whether a current level differs from levels already passed. Reverse Helmert coding asks whether a current level differs from levels still to come. Neither direction is intrinsically preferable; the linguistic comparison determines which sequence is useful.

## Reversing the MALD syllable comparisons

For the MALD syllable bands, use

$$
\mathbf C=
\begin{bmatrix}
3&0&0\\ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
-1&2&0\\
-1&-1&1\\
-1&-1&-1
\end{bmatrix},
$$

with rows ordered as one, two, three, and four-or-more syllables. The orthogonal columns encode one versus the later-band average, two versus the later-two average, and three versus four-or-more. Under this scaling, those three mean differences are respectively four, three, and two times their fitted coefficients.

For the first column, the row weights sum to zero: $3-1-1-1=0$. The coefficient thus compares one-syllable words with the three later bands rather than shifting every band together. The squared column length is $3^2+1+1+1=12$, which produces the displayed scaling; analogous weight arithmetic produces the factors three and two for the remaining columns.

To recover the named first contrast, let the fitted band means be $\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3,\mu_{4+}$. The mean of the later bands is $(\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_{4+})/3$. Their difference from the first band is

$$
\mu_1-\frac{\mu_2+\mu_3+\mu_{4+}}{3}.
$$

Under the displayed weights, this difference is four times the fitted coefficient. Writing the desired mean comparison first is the safest way to check the software scaling.

```{r}
#| label: fit-mald-reverse-helmert-coding
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mald$log_frequency_c <-
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex - mean(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$log_duration_c <- mald$log_duration - mean(mald$log_duration)
band_levels <- c(as.character(seq_len(3L)), "4+")
mald$syllable_band <- factor(
  ifelse(mald$n_syllables >= 4L, "4+", as.character(mald$n_syllables)),
  levels = band_levels
)

reverse_matrix <- matrix(
  c(3, -1, -1, -1, 0, 2, -1, -1, 0, 0, 1, -1), # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
  nrow = 4L,
  ncol = 3L
)
rownames(reverse_matrix) <- levels(mald$syllable_band)
colnames(reverse_matrix) <- c(
  "one_vs_later", "two_vs_later", "three_vs_four_plus"
)

reverse_data <- mald
contrasts(reverse_data$syllable_band) <- reverse_matrix
reverse_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_rt ~ syllable_band + log_frequency_c + log_duration_c,
  data = reverse_data
)

treatment_data <- mald
contrasts(treatment_data$syllable_band) <- contr.treatment(4)
treatment_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_rt ~ syllable_band + log_frequency_c + log_duration_c,
  data = treatment_data
)

maximum_fit_difference <- max(abs(
  fitted(reverse_fit) - fitted(treatment_fit)
))
stopifnot(maximum_fit_difference < 1e-9)

reverse_matrix
coef(summary(reverse_fit))
```

The fitted values agree to within `r format(maximum_fit_difference, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`. Reverse Helmert coding has changed the coordinate system for the category effects, not the fitted conditional means.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-reverse-helmert
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD item summaries and the fitted syllable-band means preserved by reverse Helmert coding."
prediction_data <- data.frame(
  syllable_band = factor(
    levels(reverse_data$syllable_band),
    levels = levels(reverse_data$syllable_band)
  ),
  log_frequency_c = 0,
  log_duration_c = 0
)
prediction_data$fit <- predict(reverse_fit, newdata = prediction_data)

point_opacity <- 0.06
ggplot(reverse_data, aes(syllable_band, mean_log_rt)) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey70", alpha = point_opacity, width = 0.16, height = 0, size = 0.55) +
  geom_point(data = prediction_data, aes(y = fit), color = "#2C6E9B", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Syllable-count band", y = "Mean log lexical-decision time") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The top band remains open-ended. Thus the final coefficient compares two observed bands, but it does not estimate the effect of adding exactly one syllable.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which rows receive nonzero weights in the first contrast?
2. Why do treatment and reverse Helmert coding preserve fitted values?
3. What does the final contrast compare?
4. Why is that contrast not a one-syllable causal effect?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. All four rows receive nonzero weights: 3 for the one-syllable band and -1 for each later band. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Both are full-rank bases for the same category-mean subspace, so they change coefficients but preserve fitted conditional means. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The final reverse Helmert contrast compares the fitted three-syllable mean with the fitted four-or-more-syllable mean; under the displayed scaling, that difference is twice the coefficient. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The upper band is open-ended and membership is observational, so the contrast neither adds exactly one syllable nor identifies a causal intervention. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
